item.title: How a Massachusetts cranberry farm became a thriving wetland
item.description: A former cranberry farm in Plymouth, Massachusetts, has been transformed into a thriving freshwater wetland after restoration work began in 2010. The project restored 225 acres of wetland and more than three miles of stream habitat, removed dams and barriers, and brought back native plants and wildlife. Thousands of migratory fish, including alewife and blueback herring, returned to areas they had been unable to reach for more than 100 years.

item.title: She had no claims for 10 years. Then aerial photos put her insurance at risk
item.description: Texas homeowners are increasingly finding that insurance companies are using aerial images of their properties to assess risks and decide whether to renew policies. Insurers use satellite, aircraft and third-party imagery, with some companies using AI to analyse roofs and identify possible damage. While insurers say the technology is faster and more efficient, consumer advocates warn that outdated or inaccurate images can lead to wrong decisions.

item.title: When Steve Jobs called death ‘life’s best invention’
item.description: Steve Jobs' 2005 Stanford speech emphasized death as life's greatest invention. He urged graduates to live each day as if it were their last. Jobs advised them not to waste time living someone else's life. He stressed the importance of following one's heart and intuition. This profound message continues to resonate with millions worldwide.

item.title: Lake Mead's falling water levels are revealing a US ghost town submerged by its waters 90 years ago
item.description: The receding waters of Lake Mead have unveiled the eerie remnants of St. Thomas, a ghost town in Nevada. Originally a thriving Mormon settlement founded in 1865, it was swallowed by rising waters after the Hoover Dam was built in 1938. Now, the lakebed displays its foundations, allowing history enthusiasts a rare opportunity to connect with a bygone era of agricultural significance.

item.title: Two people bitten by beavers in less than two weeks at Maryland park
item.description: At Cunningham Falls State Park, two people experienced beaver bites that resulted in positive rabies tests for both animals involved. Consequently, park authorities have restricted access to water areas to ensure public safety. Ongoing surveillance is focused on assessing the rabies situation, and restrictions will persist until health officials confirm that the park is safe for all visitors.

item.title: Singapore replaced a 2.7-km concrete canal with a winding river; biodiversity rose 30%
item.description: Singapore transformed a 2.7-km concrete canal at Bishan-Ang Mo Kio Park into a 3-km meandering river between 2009 and 2011. The project created a flood plain and more varied river habitat. Later research found 26 fish species in the rehabilitated section, including three native species, compared with eight non-native species in an untreated canal section.

item.title: Florida community fears radioactive waste pile could threaten many living nearby
item.description: Residents of Progress Village are increasingly concerned about the environmental and health threats posed by a substantial phosphogypsum stack nearby. This waste contains naturally occurring radioactive materials, raising alarms about radiation exposure and potential water contamination, particularly during storm events. Studies on the stack's effects on local air and water quality have been conducted, and the community is advocating for greater transparency and improved management of this hazardous industrial waste.

item.title: In the 1990s, Boston sent Big Dig soil to a burning dump, turning it into a park
item.description: Boston’s massive Big Dig project produced more than 16 million cubic yards of soil, and nearly a quarter of it was sent to Spectacle Island in Boston Harbor. The island was once a city dump where methane gas caused underground fires. The soil helped cap the old landfill, reshape the island and support a long restoration effort that brought back trees, plants, birds and other wildlife.
